articles.title: Band-Edge-Extended Heterointerfaces for Perovskite Solar Cells and Tandems
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11427-1Band-Edge-Extended Heterointerfaces for Perovskite Solar Cells and Tandems
articles.content: Perovskite solar cells (PSCs) have emerged as a promising photovoltaic technology, with efficiencies rapidly approaching those of established crystalline-silicon solar cells. Further efficiency gains, however, are increasingly limited by charge extraction and recombination at the interface between the perovskite absorber and the electron-transport layer. Interfacial modifiers are widely used to suppress these losses, yet many conventional ammonium-based modifiers are weakly electronically coupled to the perovskite surface and can introduce barriers to electron extraction 1-5. Here we realize electronically coupled heterointerfaces by introducing a family of heteroatom-containing, fully conjugated formamidinium interfacial modulators, establishing band-edge-extending conjugated heterointerfaces that overcome the bottleneck of inefficient interfacial electron transfer. The resulting band-edge-extended heterointerface establishes delocalized electron connectivity at the perovskite/electron transporting layer (ETL) interface and suppresses interfacial non-radiative recombination. We report a certified power-conversion efficiency (PCE) of 27.96% and a stabilized power output (SPO) of 27.84% for inverted PSCs. The corresponding devices retained over 95% of their initial efficiency after 2000 h continuous maximum-power-point tracking under 1-sun irradiation (ISOS-L). Extending this strategy to monolithic perovskite–silicon tandems enables a certified SPO of 34.71%, establishing band-edge extension as a broadly applicable approach to overcoming the conventional trade-off between interfacial passivation and charge extraction.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant breakthrough in perovskite solar cell technology, achieving very high power conversion efficiencies and long-term stability, which can contribute to more efficient and sustainable renewable energy solutions with broad societal and environmental impact.
articles.personality_title: New interface design boosts efficiency and stability of perovskite solar cells
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Perovskite solar cells are a newer type of solar technology that can convert sunlight into electricity. They have become very efficient but still face challenges where the perovskite layer meets the part that collects electrons, which can reduce how well they work.

**What happened** – Scientists created a new type of connection between the perovskite layer and the electron-collecting layer by using special molecules called formamidinium interfacial modulators. These molecules help electrons move more easily and reduce energy loss. Using this method, they made solar cells that reached nearly 28% efficiency and stayed stable for over 2,000 hours under continuous sunlight. They also applied this to combined perovskite and silicon solar cells, reaching almost 35% efficiency.

**Impact** – This is important because it solves a common problem in perovskite solar cells, improving both how much electricity they produce and how long they last. The new interface design helps electrons flow better and stops energy from being wasted, which can make solar panels more reliable and effective.

**What's next step** – Researchers will likely explore using this new interface in more types of solar cells and work on making the technology easier and cheaper to produce. This could help solar power become a more common and affordable energy source.

**One-sentence takeaway** – A new interface design significantly improves the efficiency and durability of perovskite solar cells, bringing them closer to practical, long-lasting solar energy solutions.

articles.title: How aquanauts could help save Florida’s reefs
articles.summary: With Florida’s coral facing unprecedented thermal stress, a new subsea research station gives scientists a front-row seat to monitor, protect and restore struggling ecosystems day and night
articles.content:
It sounds idyllic. Who wouldn’t want to occupy a newly built residence in the Florida Keys, complete with its own coral garden right outside the window? The only complication is that it is 17 metres below the surface of the Atlantic Ocean.

That is not putting off Jim Brittsan, though. “This is really exciting,” he says. Brittsan is the founder and executive director of coral restoration non-profit Sustainable Ocean and Reefs (SOAR). He is also the diver who arranged the temporary coral nursery beside the residence, having brought the corals from a site where, 10 metres closer to the surface, they faced increasing environmental stress. Now, in reduced temperatures, they are starting to flourish, hosting their own marine life – visible day and night, in all its busyness, from the underwater residence known as Vanguard just 15 metres away.

Vanguard was deployed at Tennessee Reef in June 2026 DEEP and Brendan Hall

Vanguard is a long-stay underwater station for marine biologists. It was deployed in June 2026 at Tennessee Reef on the seafloor of the Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary, around 8 kilometres south of Long Key. Its coral nursery looks like a strange marine shrubbery: the coral fragments are arranged on anchored ropes that stand upright in the water. Once Vanguard is operational, a more permanent nursery will be established and the corals will eventually be planted on the seabed as part of ongoing restoration efforts, with their long-term survival assessed through monitoring.

Resident scientists will be able to monitor marine life around the clock

DEEP, the international design and engineering organisation that built Vanguard, aims to make humans aquatic by establishing more subsea habitats like it. These will allow people to live underwater for extended periods to engage in scientific research and conservation. This opens up unprecedented opportunities to do research because there is no need for divers to bounce up and down to a research vessel on the surface. Those round trips eat into valuable work hours, because divers can spend only limited time at depth and must ascend slowly to avoid decompression sickness. “If we’re diving from a boat, we can do about 3 hours’ work a day at depth,” Brittsan says. “It’s much more efficient if we can just stay down there.”

Corals moved to deeper, cooler water beside Vanguard are recovering in a temporary nursery DEEP

There is plenty of work to do in the Florida Keys. Elkhorn (Acropora palmata) and staghorn (Acropora cervicornis) corals, which are vital reef-building species, are now considered functionally extinct in Florida. But it is not just in Florida waters that corals are struggling. Climate change, which brings elevated ocean temperatures, is a significant threat to corals around the world. In warmer waters, corals eject the algae that live in their tissues. This upends their mutually beneficial symbiosis in what is known as a bleaching event – without the algae and other symbionts, the corals are left a ghostly white. If temperatures do not fall and the algae do not return, the corals eventually die.

In September 2026, amid concerns about marine heat stress, SOAR received authorisation to relocate 11 different coral species to the new nursery next to Vanguard. The corals were transported using different methods depending on the species: acroporid corals were transferred submerged in bins of seawater, while other corals were moved encased in seawater-soaked bubble wrap and placed in temperature-controlled coolers. The corals were then placed in the temporary nursery in deeper water near Vanguard.

Vanguard should be fully commissioned early in 2027. After that, those transplanted corals, and their attending creatures, can be continuously monitored by aquanauts who will be living in the habitat for a week at a time.

Coral space

Brittsan and his team have also observed juvenile long-spined sea urchins (Diadema antillarum) that naturally recruited to Vanguard. “A lot of Diadema have started settling all over the habitat,” he says. This species of sea urchin is considered a keystone because its grazing reduces algal cover on reefs, providing space for corals and other reef organisms to settle and grow. That is why DEEP is taking a holistic approach, also planning to build sponge nurseries outside the habitat, for instance. “You need corals, sponges, sea urchins and everything else,” says Thomas Potts, science program director at DEEP.

Diadema urchins are particularly active at night, which means short daytime dives would miss a lot of what needs monitoring. “That’s where Vanguard really comes into play,” Potts says. Resident scientists will be able to monitor marine life around the clock.

The lessons from Vanguard will inform marine research in the Florida Keys for years to come. Vanguard is also a proving ground for DEEP’s future habitats. “It’s a great place to train scientists that might be working in different habitats on the continental shelf,” says Potts. The longer-term vision is to build a fleet of undersea residences at other locations. “This could be replicated throughout the Florida Keys and even in other parts of the world,” Brittsan says. “It’ll be a game-changer.”

articles.title: Bans cut two forever chemicals by 30 percent in England’s rivers
articles.summary:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Concentrations of PFOS and PFOA, the two most toxic forever chemicals, have fallen by 30 percent and 29 percent in England’s rivers over the past 10 years, according to new figures from the Environment Agency (EA). In freshwater fish, levels are down 49 percent. The agency attributes the decline […]
The post Bans cut two forever chemicals by 30 percent in England’s rivers first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News.
articles.content:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM

Concentrations of PFOS and PFOA, the two most toxic forever chemicals, have fallen by 30 percent and 29 percent in England’s rivers over the past 10 years, according to new figures from the Environment Agency (EA). In freshwater fish, levels are down 49 percent. The agency attributes the decline to restrictions that removed both compounds from most products, which makes the data one of the clearer measures yet of what a chemical ban does to a river system over time.

Two forever chemicals, two bans, one decade of data

PFOS and PFOA

PFAS, short for per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, were first developed in the U.S. in the 1930s. Manufacturers adopted them for their resistance to oil, water, and heat, and they ended up in nonstick pans, firefighting foam, and electrical components. The same chemical stability means they take a very long time to break down, which earned them the label forever chemicals.

PFOS and PFOA were among the earliest compounds in the family. About 20 years ago, researchers began linking them to tissue damage in animals and to higher rates of certain serious illnesses in people, including testicular cancer. The UK all but banned PFOS in 2010 and PFOA in 2020.

Results from the latest Environment Agency figures

The new data, published by the EA this month, covers 10 years of monitoring. Both chemicals declined by nearly a third in river water, while the near-halving in fish points to less of the compounds moving up the food chain. Dr. David Megson, a reader in environmental forensics at Manchester Metropolitan University, welcomed the trend. “It’s brilliant to see how far we have come in the last 10 years,” he said.

Lower concentrations, same total load

Where forever chemicals go after a ban

The EA report attaches a significant caveat to its own numbers. Because PFOS and PFOA break down so slowly, the total quantity in the environment has likely not changed much. Concentrations in rivers have dropped because the chemicals have been diluted and carried downstream into the sea. A ban stops new inputs, but it does not remove what is already circulating.

Very few methods can destroy PFAS permanently. High-temperature incineration is one of them, and England currently has only two facilities suited to the job.

Making polluters pay

Megson sees the monitoring record as a starting point for accountability. “There is a lot to do, and this report provides an essential foundation to support investigations to make the polluters pay for any damage they have caused,” he said.

Regulating PFAS as a group

15,000 compounds, 200 in common use

PFOS and PFOA are two of an estimated 15,000 PFAS, of which around 200 are in frequent use. The EA said that “uncertainty remains regarding the toxicity of many PFAS” and that its findings reinforce the case for regulating the chemicals as a class instead of one at a time. The chemicals industry has long resisted a group approach, arguing that evidence of toxicity for most other PFAS is limited or absent and that some have essential applications, including in life-saving medical equipment.

Wider monitoring

The agency now tests regularly for 60 additional PFAS to map contamination across England, and the government announced earlier this month that it will begin measuring forever chemicals in people’s bodies. Taken together with the river data, those programs will show whether the pattern seen with PFOS and PFOA holds for other compounds once restrictions arrive: a slow but steady fall in water and wildlife, with the legacy load still to be dealt with downstream.

articles.title: El Niño Rains Paint the Atacama
articles.summary: Winter precipitation helped wake dormant seeds in northern Chile, carpeting the desert with what may be the region’s most extensive flowering of the satellite era.
articles.content:
September 14 October 24 NASA Earth Observatory/Michala Garrison NASA Earth Observatory/Michala Garrison September 14 October 24 NASA Earth Observatory/Michala Garrison NASA Earth Observatory/Michala Garrison September 14 October 24 Curtain Toggle 2-Up

Parts of the Atacama Desert in northern Chile, normally one of the driest places on Earth, turned red-purple, green, and white in austral spring 2026 following an unusually wet winter. The rain woke seeds lying dormant in the soil, setting off what scientists say may be the most extensive desierto florido, or “flowering desert,” of the satellite era.

The rains came as El Niño was strengthening in the tropical Pacific. During an El Niño, the subtropical Pacific high that normally keeps the region dry weakens, while a blocking high tends to form in the South Pacific near the tip of South America. Together, these shifts push the Southern Hemisphere storm track equatorward.

Beginning in mid-July, a series of storm fronts fed by an atmospheric river brought one of the heaviest July rain events in decades to a long stretch of Chile, from the Atacama region south to Los Lagos, according to Chile’s national weather service (Dirección Meteorológica de Chile). In August, back-to-back winter storms blanketed parts of the Atacama Desert in rare snow.

The spring blooms that followed are visible in these satellite image pairs, which show the desert at different stages of flowering on September 14 (left) and on October 24 (right). The OLI (Operational Land Imager) on Landsat 8 acquired the September images, and the OLI on Landsat 9 acquired the October images.

The pair above shows a part of the desert about 30 kilometers (20 miles) southwest of Copiapó, near the eastern sector of Desierto Florido National Park. The red-purple areas prominent in the October 24 scene are vast blooms of pata de guanaco, most likely Cistanthe longiscapa or another Cistanthe species, according to Roberto Chávez, a remote sensing scientist at Pontificia Universidad Católica de Valparaíso.

Patches of red-purple Cistanthe are visible during a bloom in the Atacama Desert, shown in this photograph taken on October 24, 2026. Matías Pérez-Evens and Roberto O. Chávez/LabGRS-Instituto de Geografía- Pontificia Universidad Católica de Valparaíso.

Chávez and colleagues photographed the Cistanthe blooms (above) in the area that same day. They were in the field to study the bloom with satellite data, drones, and digital cameras. The project aims to use these data to map how the bloom’s biodiversity changes across space and over time, to inform land-use planners and conservation managers.

The pair below shows another part of the blooming desert, about 50 kilometers (30 miles) southwest of Copiapó. It lies within a priority area of the desert cited for its biological significance, including the flowering landscape.

Cistanthe is abundant here in the October view, but the September scene (left) reveals another desert beauty. The green areas capped with white are blooms of suspiros, or Nolana, probably Nolana baccata, according to Andres Moreira-Muñoz, a scientist at Pontificia Universidad Católica de Valparaíso who studies plant geography. The researchers photographed the Nolana-covered hillsides below on September 24, 2026.

White Nolana blankets a hillside in the Atacama Desert during a bloom, shown in this photograph taken on September 24, 2026. Matías Pérez-Evens and Roberto O. Chávez/LabGRS-Instituto de Geografía- Pontificia Universidad Católica de Valparaíso.

Satellite data have been key to understanding the Atacama’s blooms. A 2014 study used Landsat observations to map where flowering and fog-fed plants grow around the Copiapó dune field. And a 2019 study used NASA’s long-term vegetation record to identify 13 Atacama Desert blooms between 1981 and 2015.

Compared with those past blooms, the 2026 event stands out. “This instance of the ‘blooming desert’ phenomenon appears to be the most significant to date—in terms of its extent, intensity, and duration,” Moreira-Muñoz said, “at least since we began using remote sensing.”

articles.personality_title: El Niño rains trigger largest Atacama Desert bloom in decades
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – The Atacama Desert in northern Chile is usually one of the driest places on Earth. It rarely receives enough rain to support much plant life, and the soil seeds often lie dormant for years.

**What happened** – In the winter of 2026, unusually heavy rains arrived due to a strong El Niño weather pattern. These rains, starting in July and continuing through August, brought snow and storms that soaked the desert. As a result, dormant seeds in the soil sprouted, creating a vast and colorful bloom of flowers across the desert by spring.

**Impact** – Scientists say this bloom is the largest and most intense seen since satellites began monitoring the area. It covers wide areas with red-purple and white flowers, including species like Cistanthe and Nolana. This flowering event is important because it shows how weather changes can quickly transform a harsh desert into a vibrant ecosystem. It also helps researchers study biodiversity and plan conservation efforts.

**What's next step** – Researchers are using satellite images, drones, and cameras to map the bloom’s size and variety of plants. They aim to understand how the flowering changes over time and in different locations. This information will help protect the desert’s unique plants and guide land use decisions in the future.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Heavy El Niño rains in 2026 sparked the biggest flowering ever recorded in the Atacama Desert, turning one of Earth’s driest places into a colorful landscape and offering new insights for science and conservation.

En conséquence, des graines dormantes ont germé, créant au printemps une vaste et colorée floraison à travers le désert.

**Impact** – Les scientifiques affirment que cette floraison est la plus grande et la plus intense observée depuis que les satellites surveillent la région. Elle couvre de larges zones de fleurs rouge-pourpre et blanches, notamment des espèces comme Cistanthe et Nolana. Cet événement est important car il montre comment un changement climatique peut rapidement transformer un désert aride en un écosystème vivant. Il aide aussi les chercheurs à étudier la biodiversité et à planifier la conservation.

**Prochaine étape** – Les chercheurs utilisent des images satellites, des drones et des caméras pour cartographier la taille et la variété des plantes en fleur. Ils veulent comprendre comment la floraison change avec le temps et selon les endroits. Ces informations aideront à protéger les plantes uniques du désert et à guider les décisions d’aménagement du territoire.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Les fortes pluies d’El Niño en 2026 ont déclenché la plus grande floraison jamais enregistrée dans le désert d’Atacama, transformant l’un des endroits les plus secs de la Terre en un paysage coloré et offrant de nouvelles connaissances pour la science et la conservation.
articles.personality_title_es: Las lluvias de El Niño provocan la mayor floración del desierto de Atacama en décadas
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – El desierto de Atacama, en el norte de Chile, es normalmente uno de los lugares más secos del mundo. Rara vez recibe suficiente lluvia para que crezcan plantas, y las semillas en el suelo suelen estar dormidas durante años.

**Qué pasó** – En el invierno de 2026, fuertes lluvias llegaron debido a un fuerte fenómeno de El Niño. Estas lluvias, desde julio hasta agosto, trajeron nieve y tormentas que empaparon el desierto. Como resultado, las semillas dormidas comenzaron a crecer, creando una gran y colorida floración en la primavera.

**Impacto** – Los científicos dicen que esta floración es la más grande e intensa vista desde que los satélites comenzaron a monitorear el área. Cubre grandes zonas con flores rojo-púrpuras y blancas, incluyendo especies como Cistanthe y Nolana. Este evento es importante porque muestra cómo los cambios en el clima pueden transformar rápidamente un desierto seco en un ecosistema vivo. También ayuda a los investigadores a estudiar la biodiversidad y planear la conservación.

**Próximo paso** – Los investigadores están usando imágenes satelitales, drones y cámaras para mapear el tamaño y la variedad de plantas en flor. Quieren entender cómo cambia la floración con el tiempo y en diferentes lugares. Esta información ayudará a proteger las plantas únicas del desierto y a guiar decisiones sobre el uso de la tierra.

**Resumen en una frase** – Las fuertes lluvias de El Niño en 2026 provocaron la mayor floración registrada en el desierto de Atacama, transformando uno de los lugares más secos de la Tierra en un paisaje colorido y ofreciendo nuevas ideas para la ciencia y la conservación.
